title: Buying every 2% dip in SPY since 2000 made 29%, and fees ate a third of it
author: person-person12
selftext:
Every red day somebody in my feed says buy the dip like its a law of physics, so I wrote it down as an actual rule and ran it on SPY from January 2000 to March 2026 on daily candles, 6,599 sessions.

The rule is as dumb as the saying. If SPY closes down 2% or more from the previous close, buy the next open with the whole $10,000 account and sell at the open after that. One session held, no stop, no target, nothing else layered on. I ran it in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) with its default costs on, which for SPY is a cent a share of slippage and 50 cents commission on each side.

**Down 2% or more, 256 trades over 26 years:**

* net **+29.2%**, final equity $12,918
* 52% of trades won, profit factor 1.11
* max drawdown 27.5%
* the same trades with costs added back were **+42.6%**, so a cent a share and 50 cents a side took $1,336 off a $10,000 account

**Down 3% or more, 86 trades:**

* net **+13.6%**
* 53.5% won, profit factor 1.14
* max drawdown 16.3%

So the bounce is real, the next session after a 2% drop was up a bit more often than it was down and the average win covered the average loss with a little left over. The part nobody says out loud is how small it is. You are in the market for 256 of 6,599 sessions, about one day in 26, and 29% over 26 years is nowhere near what SPY itself did over that stretch, with a drawdown that still hit 27%.

The cost line is the one I keep looking at. Thirteen points of return went to a cent of slippage and a 50 cent commission per side, because every one of those 256 trades is a round trip on a position that is only open for a day. The edge per trade is tiny and the bill per trade is fixed, so the bill wins a third of it before you see any of it.

The first ugly one in the 2% version was buying the open after a down day in April 2000 and watching it fall another 3.3% into the next morning, $344 gone on a $10,000 account in one session. Two trading days later the same rule fired again and made $397.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the 29% vs SPY comparison flatters SPY a bit, since the money sits idle 25 sessions out of 26. park that idle cash in T-bills and the gap shrinks a lot, though a 27% drawdown on roughly one day a month of exposure still stings. how many of the 256 came from 2008 and March 2020?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: fair on the T-bills, the idle cash earned nothing in this run so the real gap to SPY is smaller than it looks. the crisis years didnt carry it tho, 2008 was 34 of the 256 trades and lost $216, 2020 was 22 trades and lost $88. **2000 and 2001 alone made $4,338**, more than the whole run netted, and everything from 2002 on lost about $1,420 combined.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: so two years did the whole job and everything from 2002 on lost money. a single total hides that completely. it's why I made Quantradin show every rule's result year by year (free, paper money, quantradin.com).

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea thats the part that bugged me most about it. **29% sounds like a result** until you see two years carried the whole thing and the rest of the run slowly handed it back.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, and a dip rule is exactly the kind a total flatters, because the crashes hand it the best dips. I'd want to see it run with those two years cut out before trusting any of the 29%.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Funny thing is cutting those two out barely moves it, 2008 and 2020 both finished slightly red on this rule. **Almost all of the 29% came from 2000 and 2001**, and from 2002 on it was net negative, so the dot com unwind is what flatters the total.

comments.author: Electrical_Waltz_888
comments.body:
Writing “buy the dip” as an explicit rule makes this much more useful than the slogan.

How did you treat the cash between trades? With the strategy invested for only 256 sessions, earning interest on the remaining cash could materially change the account-level result. Buy-and-hold is useful context, but the exposure is very different.

I’d also be cautious about “the bounce is real”. These results show a positive historical return under the stated assumptions; they don’t establish that it persists. Did most of the gains come from a few crisis periods, or was the result reasonably consistent across different periods?

Disclosure: I wrote The Complete Guide to AI Powered Trading, which covers turning informal ideas into testable rules and questioning what backtests establish. This is exactly the kind of discussion it focuses on.

[https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HNM97TQ9](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HNM97TQ9)

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Cash sat idle between trades with no interest on it, so yea the account level number understates it and buy and hold is a different exposure entirely. On consistency it was close to the opposite of a few crisis periods carrying it, 2008 and 2020 both finished slightly red and **almost all of the gain came from 2000 and 2001**. From 2002 to now the same rule was net negative, which is a fair hit on the bounce line.
